front: What is pandas in one sentence?
back: Columnar DataFrame library for load → transform → analyze → export workflows in Python.

front: Explain the mental model of pandas (how the system thinks).
back: A DataFrame is labeled columns (Series) with a shared index. Operations are vectorized (C-backed) when possible. Missing data is NaN. Dtype matters: object vs int vs category affects memory and speed. Prefer explicit dtypes on ingest for prod pipelines.

front: Symptom: SettingWithCopyWarning — what do you check and fix?
back: Check: Chained indexing · Fix: Use .loc[] assignment

front: Symptom: Memory blowup — what do you check and fix?
back: Check: df.memory_usage(deep=True) · Fix: Downcast dtypes; read columns subset

front: Symptom: Merge explosion — what do you check and fix?
back: Check: Key duplicates · Fix: validate="m:1"; dedupe keys

front: Symptom: NaN after math — what do you check and fix?
back: Check: Dtype object · Fix: Coerce numeric first

front: Symptom: Slow loop over rows — what do you check and fix?
back: Check: iterrows · Fix: Vectorize or .apply axis=0 sparingly

front: Gotcha with pandas: what silently fails?
back: fillna(0) after coerce — hides bad data; log/coerce count first in ETL. CSV locale commas — specify decimal=',' for EU files. Timezone-naive datetimes — always UTC in storage.

front: When should you NOT use pandas?
back: Don't use pandas for row-by-row OLTP — use SQL/ORM. Don't load 100GB CSV on a laptop — use DuckDB/Polars/spark for out-of-core.

front: What is Python wheel (.whl) in one sentence?
back: Built distribution format — pre-built zip of code + metadata for fast pip install without compile on target.

front: Explain the mental model of Python wheel (.whl) (how the system thinks).
back: sdist (source tarball) may compile C extensions on install. wheel ships pre-built artifacts for a platform tag (cp312-manylinux_x86_64). pip prefers wheels when tag matches. You build wheels in CI; consumers install in seconds.

front: Which standard commands / workflow do you use for Python wheel (.whl)?
back: pyproject.toml / setup.py → build backend → dist/*.whl → pip install → pip install build → python -m build # produces dist/*.whl and *.tar.gz → pip install dist/mypackage-0.1.0-py3-none-any.whl → pip install setuptools wheel

front: Given a broken Python wheel (.whl) setup, what is your first validation command?
back: pyproject.toml / setup.py → build backend → dist/*.whl → pip install

front: Symptom: not a supported wheel — what do you check and fix?
back: Check: Platform tag · Fix: Build on target arch or use pure py3-none-any

front: Symptom: Compile on install anyway — what do you check and fix?
back: Check: No wheel for platform · Fix: Publish manylinux wheel via cibuildwheel

front: Symptom: Wrong version installed — what do you check and fix?
back: Check: PyPI name clash · Fix: Unique package name; pin in requirements

front: Symptom: Import error after install — what do you check and fix?
back: Check: Package layout · Fix: packages= in setuptools config

front: Symptom: Huge wheel — what do you check and fix?
back: Check: Bundled data · Fix: Exclude tests; use MANIFEST.in carefully

front: Gotcha with Python wheel (.whl): what silently fails?
back: Manylinux vs musl (Alpine) — glibc wheels fail on Alpine; use slim Debian base or build musllinux wheel. Commit wheels to git — usually wrong; publish to index or artifact store. setup.py only projects — migrate to pyproject.toml for reproducible builds.

front: When should you NOT use Python wheel (.whl)?
back: Don't hand-edit wheel contents — rebuild from source. Don't ship platform-specific wheels as py3-none-any — runtime import errors.
